messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Error about Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
parts:
Hi,

Please start by following the instructions in the error message to rerun inla() with verbose=TRUE, since that may reveal more information, e.g. if the theta values were diverging or otherwise abnormal.  Optimiser errors usually happen because of badly shaped likelihoods, so please also provide more details on the precise model you were trying to estimate.

Finn L

Thank you for the verbose-output; it indicates that not even the initial
values for the theta-parameters give a valid precision matrix.

> I use the spde-model with some other bases functions phi in x=sum
> c-j*phi-j as my tutor told me by changing the matrices in the output of
> inla.spde2.matern, param.inla$M0 M1 M2, he asked me to ask for help
> here, thanks a lot in advance.

Currently, changing M* in param.inla of the spde-object will not have
the desired effect in inla() unless you also write those matrices to
disk in the appropriate way, and an easier approach is to use
inla.spde2.generic() instead to setup you model. However, both
approaches require that the resulting model gives positive definite
precision matrices.

Fortunately, changing the spde object (without writing the matrices to
disk) will still allow the functions implemented in R to work with the
object:
Use
Q = inla.spde2.precision(spde, theta=c(0,0))
to obtain the precision matrix for theta at zero, and check the
eigenvalues with
eigen(Q, only.values=TRUE)
They should all be positive. If they are, also check with other
theta-combinations. If they aren't, then you M*-matrices do not
generate a valid model.

Finn

> Thanks a lot!
> You are totally right, Q is not positive definite. My C_{ii} = \sum_j
> C_{ij} can be negative...
> It seems that I have to consider how to ensure the positive definiteness...

If you constructed the matrices from scalar products of basis functions
and gradients of basis functions, like for finite elements, the
resulting Q should have been positive definite, which indicates that you
have made a mistake in your calculations, so start by checking those...

Finn

> Thanks a lot!
> You are totally right, Q is not positive definite. My C_{ii} = \sum_j
> C_{ij} can be negative...
> It seems that I have to consider how to ensure the positive definiteness...

Also, the "replace C by a diagonal matrix" is mostly appropriate for
very local basis functions, so it may not be appropriate for other
choices of basis. (E.g., for higher order b-spline basis functions one
can use the least squares construction method instead of galerkin, which
gives a valid approximation that is still sparse. In the JRSSB
spde/gmrf 2011 paper, the least squares method was used for the alpha=1
case)

Finn
